title: The summer solstice
hook: the longest day, and Marcus would note it passes too

segments.voice: Yesterday: a neighbor's day of atonement, and a question it leaves for anyone watching with respect. Your line was honest review. Did one honest look, or one honest message, happen? Day six hundred sixty-nine.

Nine-thirty at night, and it's still light enough to read on the back step. Kids are still out on bikes. Somebody's grill is still going. In the far north, in places like northern Norway, the sun doesn't set at all this time of year. The summer solstice: the longest day in the northern half of the world. People have lit bonfires for it, danced around poles for it, stayed up all night for it. The light seems like it could go on forever. Marcus Aurelius would enjoy it, and then gently remind himself of one thing.
screen: `STILL LIGHT AT NINE-THIRTY.` → `THE LONGEST DAY.` → `IT SEEMS TO GO ON FOREVER.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Solstice comes from Latin, solstitium: the sun standing still. For days around it, the sun seems to rise and set at almost the same points on the horizon, as if pausing at the top of its climb before turning back. Second, the pause is the turn. From tomorrow, in the north, the days begin to shorten, a little at a time. The peak of the light and the start of its going are the same moment. Third, Marcus. He writes in the Meditations that time is like a river made of things that happen, a strong current: as soon as something is seen, it's swept away, and something else takes its place, and that too will be carried off. He also tells himself to think often about how fast everything that exists and comes into being is carried past and out of sight. To some readers that sounds bleak. But read beside his other notes, it's not a reason to hold back from enjoying things. It's a reason to enjoy them now, while they're here, without trying to clamp them in place. Fourth, the solstice as practice. A long day can seem so roomy that it slips by unnoticed. Marcus's reminder turns that around: because it's passing, it's worth being out in. Long light, still passing. Both halves are true, and the second makes the first worth more.
screen: `SOLSTITIUM: THE SUN STANDING STILL.` · `THE PEAK IS ALSO THE TURN.` · `A RIVER OF THINGS, SWEPT PAST.` · `PASSING, SO WORTH BEING OUT IN.` · then, large: `LONG LIGHT, STILL PASSING.`

segments.voice: If you can, go outside, or sit by a window with the most sky you can find. Look at the light as it is right now. Its color. Where the shadows fall. How warm or cool the air is. Let yourself enjoy it fully, without planning anything. Then, quietly, notice that this exact light is already changing, moving across the wall, the ground, your hand. Enjoy it anyway, and partly because it's passing. The bell holds the time.
The summer solstice: the longest day, when the sun seems to stand still before the days start shortening, a moment of full light that is already turning. Today's word.
Your line: long light, still passing. Spend ten minutes of today's light outdoors on purpose, not on the way to anywhere. Day six hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Many cultures mark midsummer with bonfires, outdoor gatherings or staying up through the short night; some readers of Marcus use the longest day as a reminder to enjoy what is passing.

what it means: it's the peak and the turning point at once; the light is full and already leaving.
what a scholar hears: sol plus sistere, to make stand; Meditations 4.43 calls time a river of events and a violent current, and 5.23 asks him to think how fast all things are carried past.
